rows.subtype: Not studying so failure has an excuse [Actor]
rows.description: A child says they didn't even try before an exam they fear; low effort protects the sense of being clever if the mark is poor.

rows.subtype: Staying up late before a big match [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager who fears losing stays up gaming the night before and blames tiredness afterwards; the handicap gives a ready excuse but also hurts the actual chance.

rows.subtype: Leaving an assignment for the last night [Actor]
rows.description: A student postpones a paper and declares it was done in a rush, so a low grade says nothing about ability; the person wins a little face and loses the chance to learn.
A child keeps eating food he dislikes because it was paid for or keeps playing a boring game because he has already spent an hour. Past effort feels like a reason to continue.

rows.subtype: Stuck in coaching or a course [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager continues a subject or a coaching class he hates because of the fees and years already invested. Fear of wasting the past costs him his future time.
A student stays in a degree or relationship that no longer fits because leaving would make earlier years feel wasted. The past cannot be recovered but the future can still be chosen.

rows.subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
rows.description: A child in a noisy crowd at a fair or match shouts and pushes with everyone else. Crowd energy feels contagious and personal responsibility fades.

rows.subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
rows.description: A teenager adds a mocking comment to a viral post because many others are doing so. Anonymity and numbers make it feel harmless, though the target sees every word.

rows.subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
rows.description: A young adult at a protest, match or festival feels bolder and less accountable. The sense of being one of many can free courage, but also permits acts they would never do alone.
A child who gets to decide and see the result, such as planting a seed or fixing a toy, learns that actions matter; agency grows from evidence that effort changes things.
A teenager facing a hard family situation lists what is in their control, such as study time and who to talk to, and what is not; acting on the first list restores a sense of power.

A teenager faces persuasion to try risky things and can say no, suggest another plan, blame a rule or leave. A good friend accepts a refusal; repeated pressure is a reason to seek an adult or new company.
A young adult offers a middle path that lets each side keep dignity, such as a trial period or a split. Framing it around shared goals and acknowledging concessions usually helps.
A young child watches puja, aarti, birthday songs or a candle blown out and learns that certain actions mark special moments. Explaining why the ritual matters helps meaning grow beyond imitation.

A young adult reads a wedding baraat, a religious procession, a graduation march or a funeral cortege as marking joy, devotion or loss. Meaning is set by tradition, so an outsider observes respectfully and asks.
